In everyday life, time is often understood as a linear progression, where each moment follows sequentially from the previous one. We measure and divide it into units such as seconds, minutes, hours, days, and years to structure our lives and make sense of the world around us. This linear perspective allows us to plan, remember, and anticipate events.

However, the understanding of time shifts when we delve into the realm of physics. According to Einstein's theory of relativity, time is not an absolute entity but is relative to the observer's motion and gravitational field. In this view, time can dilate or contract, meaning that time passes slower for an object moving at high speeds or in a stronger gravitational field compared to a stationary or less gravitationally influenced object. This concept challenges the idea of a single, universal flow of time and introduces the notion of time as a dimension that can be warped by physical phenomena.
